archetype.name: Pocket Passer (big-arm, under siege)
archetype.definition: A 6-foot-6 rhythm-and-arm passer who has always won from the pocket and runs mostly when it breaks down, now stuck behind a leaky line in the league's most run-heavy offense.

report.headline: A good passer buried by a broken offense, and now pressing through it.
report.take:
Herbert's track record is a reliable above-average starter: positive EPA per play in every season from 2020 to 2025, peaking at 0.199 in 2021 and sitting at 0.09 last year, with CPOE above zero in four of those six years. This season he is 43rd of 47 in EPA per dropback at -0.26, against a league average of 0.034, and the Chargers haven't won a game he has started. That is a collapse, and the useful question is how much of it belongs to him.

The context is brutal. The offense ranks 32nd in EPA, 32nd in success rate and 31st in hit rate allowed, and Jim Harbaugh's team passes 11.1 points less often than situations call for, also last in the league. Herbert is throwing into obvious passing downs from behind schedule: third downs average 8.9 yards to go, and his third-down EPA is -0.29. His bad-throw rate of 14.2% is only 0.9 points worse than last year's and right in his career range, yet his CPOE has fallen 5.8 points. The ball isn't leaving his hand much worse. The throws he's being asked to make, and what happens after the catch, are. The clearest sign is the short game. Throws behind the line return -0.273 EPA on 47 attempts, and throws under 10 air yards return -0.19. Throws of 10-plus yards come out near neutral at -0.015 even with 8 of his 10 interceptions in that bucket.

What the line hides is how much of the damage comes from two things: sacks and late-game meltdowns. His pressure rate of 24.9% isn't extreme, but 36.2% of those pressures become sacks. That number has climbed for most of his career, from 17.1% as a rookie to 33.3% in 2024, so holding the ball when nothing is open is now part of who he is, not a 2026 blip. In close fourth quarters he has 28 plays, 9 sacks and -1.155 EPA per play, which is most of the gap between bad and catastrophic. The interceptions are the other half: 4.7% of his throws, worst-tier, after 13 picks last year showed the risk was already there.

The direction is worrying. His game EPA has gotten worse almost every week, and in Week 8 he shrank to a 5.0-yard intended air distance and a 3.1% aggressiveness rate. He completed 24 of 32 with a +4.3 CPOE and still posted -16.2 EPA with two picks. Dinking didn't fix it. He is a better quarterback than this, but the structure around him isn't improving fast, and he is pressing.

strengths.title: Downfield throws still hold value
strengths.body: His 10-plus-yard throws come out near neutral (-0.015 EPA) and succeed 45% of the time, despite carrying 8 interceptions. The arm and the willingness to drive intermediate windows are intact; the short game is what bleeds points. This is his career profile, so it should last, and it is the part of his game the offense should lean into.

strengths.title: Wideouts are producing when targeted
strengths.body: McConkey (0.389 EPA/target), Harris (0.3) and Johnston (0.244) are all comfortably positive. The losses come from tight end Oronde Gadsden II at -0.337 on 26 targets. The left side of the field also works at +0.195 per attempt. His reads to the receivers are paying; the volume to the tight end and to the right side isn't.

strengths.title: Legs keep a fantasy floor
strengths.body: He ranks 6th among qualifiers in rushing yards, and scrambles are slightly positive at 0.028 EPA each. Last year he ran for 498 yards, 2nd at the position, so this is a real and stable part of his game. It props up his output even when the passing sinks.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks too often
concerns.body: A 36.2% pressure-to-sack rate behind a line that ranks 31st in hits allowed drives a 9.8% sack rate, 2.9 points over the league average. Part of this is the line. Part is him: that rate has risen across his career, and he still holds the ball 2.81 seconds. With a starting guard out, expect no quick fix.

concerns.title: Close-game collapse and turnovers
concerns.body: In one-score games he is at -0.393 EPA per play with 7 of his 10 interceptions. In close fourth quarters he is at -1.155 with 9 sacks on 28 plays. Five interceptions on 51 intermediate throws is a forcing problem, the cost of chasing from behind in an offense that can't stay on schedule. Some of the interception rate should cool on bigger samples, but the pattern fits his history of double-digit picks.

concerns.title: Short game is broken
concerns.body: Screens and throws behind the line return -0.273 EPA with a -7.7 CPOE, and throws to the right side are at -0.345 on 105 attempts. That points to scheme, blocking and yards after the catch more than his accuracy. It still caps his efficiency as long as the staff keeps leaning on it.

trend.note: His game passing EPA has worsened nearly every week, from near-even in Week 2 to -14 and -16.2 in the last two games. His last three games sit 0.13 EPA per dropback below a season that was already poor. Week 8's ultra-short approach (5.0 intended air yards) raised his completion rate and didn't stop the slide.

nextGame.headline: Houston's secondary gives up big plays; its pass rush is the catch.
nextGame.body:
Houston's pass defense fits what Herbert still does well. The Texans rank 22nd in pass EPA allowed, dead last in explosive pass rate allowed and 26th on deep throws. They give quarterbacks 270.1 yards a game, 25th in the league, and offenses pass against them more than usual (passRateOverNorm 4th). The opposing WR1 and WR2 have beaten their averages here, while tight ends have been held well under theirs. That lines up with his strong wideout production and his struggles going to Gadsden. The problem is the rush: Houston's 7.7% sack rate ranks 5th, against a quarterback who turns pressure into sacks at a high rate. The Book makes the Chargers 4.5-point home underdogs with a low 40.5 total, so it expects a grind.

Availability cuts both ways. Starting guard Kayode Awosika (69% of snaps) is out, which thins a line already 31st in hits allowed right when it faces a top-five sack unit. David Njoku remains on IR and the 21-day practice window may only open this week, so the tight end group stays as is. Brenen Thompson's absence barely touches the passing game. On Houston's side, both starting safeties are questionable: Jalen Pitre (92% of snaps, shoulder) and Reed Blankenship (86%, concussion and hand surgery). If either sits, the deep middle of a defense already 26th on deep throws gets softer still.

keyMatchups.title: Houston's rush vs a depleted line
keyMatchups.body: The Texans' sack rate ranks 5th, and Herbert's pressure-to-sack rate is 36.2% with a guard out. Drive-killing sacks are what has sunk his close-game numbers. Quick, defined throws to the wideouts, not screens, are the counter.

keyMatchups.title: Explosive plays against weakened safeties
keyMatchups.body: Houston allows the league's highest explosive pass rate and ranks 26th on deep EPA, and both starting safeties are questionable. His 10-plus-yard throws are his most efficient, so this is the week to push the ball rather than repeat Week 8's checkdown plan.

keyMatchups.title: Wideouts over the tight end
keyMatchups.body: Houston's WR1 and WR2 numbers rank 27th and 30th, while it holds TE1s well under their averages. Herbert's wideouts all carry positive EPA per target and Gadsden doesn't. The target split should tilt toward McConkey, Harris and Johnston.

nextGame.watch: His intended air yards: if he attacks Houston's leaky secondary instead of the Week 8 checkdown plan, this is his best chance at a positive passing day in weeks.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect better than this, but not his old self. His 2.4% touchdown rate sits 2.2 points under the league average, and a career-long positive passer should climb back toward something closer to normal. The interception rate should also ease from extreme levels, though his history says it won't get low. What looks structural is everything around him. The league's most run-heavy, least efficient offense caps his volume near 30 attempts a game. A line that ranks 31st in hits allowed, paired with his own rising sack tendency, keeps the sack rate high. The broken short game drags his efficiency regardless of how well he throws downfield.

A realistic path is roughly 190 to 235 passing yards with around one touchdown a game, about a pick a game, and 20 to 35 rushing yards keeping a modest fantasy floor. Upside depends on the staff letting him throw more against soft secondaries. Downside is that the Week 8 conservatism becomes the plan and the line keeps losing bodies.
swingFactors: Offensive line health and pass protection
Whether the staff lets him throw downfield more
Tight end usage shifting toward the wideouts

confidence.note: Seven games of a consistent slide, but it clashes with six seasons of a competent career and rests on a team context that could change.
